parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the centre of gravity of an object.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what weight really is - the combined pull of gravity on every tiny particle of the object, and where you could replace all of that with a single force.
parts.proper_answer: The centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight of the object may be considered to act.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the whole weight in one place**
Imagine every atom in the object has its own tiny weight pulling down. It would be very messy to draw them all, so in physics you replace them by one single weight force $W$ acting at one special point. That point is the centre of gravity.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Two blocks are on a horizontal beam that is pivoted at its centre of gravity, as shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

A large block of weight $54\text{ N}$ is a distance of $0.45\text{ m}$ from the pivot. A small block of weight $2.4\text{ N}$ is a distance of $0.95\text{ m}$ from the pivot and a distance of $0.35\text{ m}$ from the right-hand end of the beam.

The right-hand end of the beam is connected to the ground by a string that is at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The beam is in equilibrium.
parts.text: By taking moments about the pivot, calculate the tension $T$ in the string.

markscheme_points.text: (kg m^-3 x s) / (kg x m) = kg m^-1 s^-1

hints: Hint 1: For equilibrium about the pivot, clockwise moments must balance anticlockwise moments. Identify which weights try to turn the beam each way.
Hint 2: Only the component of $T$ perpendicular to the beam contributes to the moment. What is the vertical component of a force $T$ at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal?
Hint 3: Write anticlockwise moment = clockwise moments using the correct distances from the pivot, especially the distance of the string end, then solve for $T$.
parts.proper_answer: Anticlockwise moment $= 54 \times 0.45 = 24.3\text{ N m}$. Clockwise moments $= 2.4 \times 0.95 + T\sin30^{\circ} \times 1.30$. For equilibrium $T\sin30^{\circ} \times 1.30 + 2.28 = 24.3$, giving $T = 34\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the principle of moments about the pivot**
You are sitting beside the beam. For balance, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment. Taking moments about the pivot is clever because the pivot force then has zero moment.

Step 2: **Find each moment**
Left 54 N weight pulls down 0.45 m left of pivot:
$$M_{anti} = 54 \times 0.45 = 24.3\text{ N m}$$
Right 2.4 N weight pulls down 0.95 m right of pivot:
$$M_{1} = 2.4 \times 0.95 = 2.28\text{ N m}$$
The string is at the right-hand end, distance from pivot:
$$d = 0.95 + 0.35 = 1.30\text{ m}$$
Only the vertical part causes a moment about the horizontal beam. Resolve $T$:
$$T_{v} = T\sin30^{\circ} \text{ downwards}$$
So its moment is:
$$M_{2} = T\sin30^{\circ} \times 1.30$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The string is cut so that the beam is no longer in equilibrium.

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant moment about the pivot acting on the beam immediately after the string is cut.

markscheme_points.text: L contributes 2% so R contributes more (to the

hints: Hint 1: Immediately after cutting, the tension moment disappears but the two weights still act where they did - so find anticlockwise minus clockwise moments.
parts.proper_answer: Resultant moment $= 54 \times 0.45 - 2.4 \times 0.95 = 22\text{ N m}$ anticlockwise, magnitude $22\text{ N m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remove the string term**
Once the string is cut, $T = 0$. The beam is no longer balanced. The resultant moment is just the difference of the weight moments:
$$M_{res} = 54 \times 0.45 - 2.4 \times 0.95$$
$$M_{res} = 24.3 - 2.28 = 22\text{ N m}$$
Its direction is anticlockwise, so the left side goes down.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The beam in (b) rotates when the string is cut and the small block of weight $2.4\text{ N}$ is projected through the air. Fig. 2.2 shows the last part of the path of the block before it hits the ground at point $Y$.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}

Fig. 2.2 (not to scale)

At point $X$ on the path, the block has a speed of $3.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and is at a height of $1.8\text{ m}$ above the horizontal ground. Air resistance is negligible.
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in the gravitational potential energy of the block for its movement from $X$ to $Y$.

markscheme_points.text: (of the object) is taken to act

hints: Hint 1: Recall how loss of gravitational potential energy is linked to weight and vertical drop, not to the curved path length.
Hint 2: Use the given weight 2.4 N directly with the vertical fall of 1.8 m from X to Y to get energy in joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link weight to potential energy**
Gravitational potential energy change is $mg\Delta h$. But $mg$ is just the weight $W$. Here $W = 2.4\text{ N}$ and the vertical drop from X to ground Y is $h = 1.8\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$\Delta E_{p} = W h = 2.4 \times 1.8 = 4.32\text{ J}$$
$$\approx 4.3\text{ J}$$
This energy is lost as the block falls.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Use your answer to (c)(i) and conservation of energy to determine the kinetic energy of the block at $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: With no air resistance, lost gravitational potential energy becomes extra kinetic energy, so KE at Y = KE at X + decrease from (c)(i).
Hint 2: To get KE at X you need mass, but you are given weight. How are mass and weight related through $g$?
Hint 3: Calculate $E_{kX} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ with $m = W/g$ and $v = 3.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$, then add the 4.3 J.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply conservation of energy**
No air resistance means no work lost to heat. So:
$$E_{kY} = E_{kX} + \text{loss in } E_{p}$$

Step 2: **Find kinetic energy at X**
First get mass from weight:
$$m = \frac{W}{g} = \frac{2.4}{9.81} = 0.245\text{ kg}$$
Then:
$$E_{kX} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.245 \times (3.4)^{2}$$
$$E_{kX} = 1.4\text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Add the gained energy**
$$E_{kY} = 1.4 + 4.3 = 5.7\text{ J}$$
The block speeds up as it falls, so KE at the ground is larger.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: State the variation, if any, in the direction of the acceleration of the block as it moves from $X$ to $Y$.

markscheme_points.text: no variation or acceleration is (always) vertically downwards

hints: Hint 1: Think about what force acts on the block in the air when air resistance is negligible - what direction is that force always in?
parts.proper_answer: No variation. Acceleration is always vertically downwards at $g$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Only gravity acts**
Once projected, with air resistance negligible, the only force is weight straight down. By $F = ma$, acceleration is therefore always in the same direction as weight - vertically downwards with magnitude $g$ - even while the block moves along its curved path.

parts.text:
The block passes point $X$ at time $t_X$ and arrives at point $Y$ at time $t_Y$.

On Fig. 2.3, sketch a graph to show the variation of the magnitude of the horizontal component of the velocity of the block with time from $t_X$ to $t_Y$. Numerical values are not required.

{{figure:figure_2_3}}

Fig. 2.3

markscheme_points.text: horizontal straight line at a non-zero value of velocity

hints: Hint 1: Consider whether there is any horizontal force or horizontal acceleration to change the horizontal part of the velocity.
parts.proper_answer: Horizontal straight line at a constant non-zero value from $t_{X}$ to $t_{Y}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Horizontal motion has no force**
There is no horizontal force (no air resistance), so horizontal acceleration is zero. That means the horizontal component of velocity stays constant. On the axes, draw a flat horizontal line starting above zero at $t_{X}$ and ending at $t_{Y}$.
